lessons.title: Study Session 1: Deciding What Actually Needs Her

blocks.text: Introduction Halima Idi forwarded nearly everything to her executive director, certain that flagging every decision showed diligence, until her director asked her, plainly, why he was being consulted on a routine vendor invoice he had never once needed to see. This session is about learning to tell the difference between what genuinely needs an executive's own attention and what does not. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Distinguish work only the executive can do from work that can be handled elsewhere. Explain why over-forwarding decisions undermines an executive's real effectiveness. Triage incoming items by whether they require the executive's judgment. Escalate appropriately rather than defaulting to either extreme. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Diligence That Missed the Point Halima Idi supports the executive director of an agricultural development organization in Niamey, and for her first several months she forwarded nearly every decision to him, certain that flagging everything proved she was thorough. Her director, increasingly buried in routine approvals, finally asked her directly why a standard vendor invoice, one that matched an already-approved budget line, needed his personal sign-off at all. 2.2 The Few Things Only the Executive Can Do In 1966, Peter Drucker published The Effective Executive, the first book to define systematically what effectiveness actually requires of someone in a senior role. Drucker's central argument is that an executive's real contribution comes from a small number of decisions and relationships that genuinely require their own judgment, and that effectiveness depends on protecting that limited attention for exactly those few things, while everything that can be handled by someone else genuinely should be, not out of laziness, but because an executive's attention spent on routine matters is attention not spent on what only they can actually do. 2.3 Triaging What Actually Needs Her Naming What Genuinely Requires the Executive's Judgment A decision that depends on information, relationships, or authority only the executive holds belongs with the executive; a decision that any competent person with clear guidelines could make does not. Distinguishing Diligence From Over-Forwarding Forwarding every item regardless of whether it needs the executive's specific judgment is not actually thoroughness; it is a failure to do the triage the role exists to provide. Escalating the Genuinely Uncertain Cases Appropriately When an item's status is genuinely unclear, a brief, specific question, does this need your input or can I proceed under the existing policy, resolves the uncertainty faster than either forwarding blindly or deciding unilaterally without checking. 2.4 Key Practices Ask, of each incoming item, whether it genuinely requires the executive's own judgment. Handle routine matters that fit existing guidelines without forwarding them unnecessarily. Escalate genuinely uncertain items with a specific question, not a vague forward. Review periodically which categories of decision could shift from escalated to routine. 2.5 A Worked Example: Halima's New Triage List After her director's question, Halima built a short written list, developed with him directly, naming which categories of decision she could handle under existing policy, routine invoices matching an approved budget line, standard travel requests under a set amount, and which genuinely needed his input, anything involving a new vendor, anything above a defined threshold, anything touching a partner relationship. Within a month, her director's inbox of routine approvals had genuinely thinned, and the items that did reach him were, without exception, ones that actually needed his judgment. Halima had not become less careful. She had become more precise about where her care was actually needed. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Equating forwarding everything with being thorough is the assumption that quietly overwhelms even a well-intentioned executive's schedule, because it treats every item as equally deserving of their limited attention, most of which never actually needed it. Genuine diligence means sorting correctly, not simply passing everything along unsorted. 2.7 Protecting What Only She Can Protect Halima's triage list did not make her job smaller. It made the small part of her director's week that genuinely needed him arrive clearly labelled as such, instead of buried inside everything else that did not. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to triage incoming items by whether they genuinely require an executive's own judgment, rather than forwarding everything by default. This prepares you for Study Session 2, where the same discipline shapes how you structure a briefing document once something does need the executive's attention.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Name one recurring decision you currently escalate that could actually be handled under existing guidelines. 2. Draft one specific question you could ask to resolve a genuinely uncertain item, rather than forwarding it blindly. Practical Output: Practical Output A short written triage list naming at least three categories of routine decision and three categories that genuinely require an executive's own judgment. 7.0 References and Further Reading Drucker, P.F. (1966). The Effective Executive. New York: Harper & Row. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Exodus 18:21-22, on Jethro's advice to Moses to appoint capable people over routine matters, bringing only the hard cases to him. Qur'an, Surah An-Naml 27:32-33, on the Queen of Sheba consulting her council before deciding a weighty matter.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Leading With the Conclusion

blocks.text: Introduction Yves Kouassi wrote briefing notes the way he had once written university essays, building carefully toward a conclusion his executive was expected to reach only at the very end. His executive, reading between two other meetings, never got there. This session focuses on structuring a briefing so its main point survives even the most rushed possible read. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain why a busy executive needs a document's conclusion first. Group supporting points logically beneath a main message. Distinguish a pyramid structure from a chronological narrative. Test whether a briefing survives a thirty-second read. Revise a dense briefing into a layered one. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Conclusion Nobody Reached Yves Kouassi prepares briefing notes for a bank executive in Abidjan, and his early briefings read like careful arguments, background first, then analysis, then, finally, a recommendation in the closing paragraph. His executive, who often read briefings in the gaps between back-to-back meetings, regularly stopped partway through, having absorbed the background but never reached the actual point Yves had been building toward. 2.2 The Mind Sorts Into Pyramids In 1987, Barbara Minto, a former McKinsey consultant, published The Pyramid Principle, arguing that the human mind naturally organizes information into pyramidal groupings to make sense of it, and that writing which respects this structure, a single governing point stated first, with supporting groups of ideas arranged beneath it, is grasped far faster than writing that builds gradually toward its point. Her approach became standard training at major consulting firms specifically because it lets a reader absorb the main message immediately, then choose how deep to go into the supporting detail. 2.3 Building a Document as a Pyramid, Not a Story Stating the Governing Point First Opening with the single conclusion or recommendation a document exists to deliver, rather than the reasoning that led there, means a reader who stops after one sentence still has the point. Grouping Supporting Ideas Logically Beneath It Organizing supporting detail into a small number of clear groups, each answering a natural question the main point raises, rather than a loose sequence of observations, lets a reader go deeper only where they need to. Testing the Document Against a Rushed Read Reading a finished briefing as though only its first sentence would actually be read reveals whether the document's real point survives a reader with thirty seconds, rather than thirty minutes. 2.4 Key Practices State the governing conclusion or recommendation in the very first sentence. Group supporting points into a small number of logical categories beneath the main point. Test a briefing by imagining a reader who only reads the first sentence. Reserve chronological narrative for background, never for the document's actual point. Revise any document where the main point does not appear until the final paragraph. 2.5 A Worked Example: Yves's Briefing, Restructured Yves's old briefing on a proposed loan restructuring opened with three paragraphs of account history before finally recommending, in the fourth paragraph, that the bank approve a revised repayment schedule. His executive had stopped reading before reaching it twice. His revised briefing opens with one sentence: Recommend approving a revised repayment schedule for Client X, extending the term by eight months. Three short groups follow, financial rationale, risk considerations, and client relationship impact, each a few sentences a reader could stop after if satisfied. His executive approved the recommendation from a hallway conversation, having read only the opening line and one supporting group. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Building a document the way a careful argument is built, background, then analysis, then conclusion, is the instinct that fails most often in executive briefing, because it assumes a reader who will patiently follow the whole structure through to the end, when in practice very few actually will. A document's real conclusion belongs at the top, not as its reward for reading everything else first. 2.7 The Point First, Not the Reward for Reading On Yves's briefings did not become simpler once he restructured them, only more forgiving of exactly how little time his executive actually had, which turned out to be the entire difference between a recommendation read and one abandoned halfway through. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to structure a briefing as a pyramid, stating the governing point first and grouping supporting detail logically beneath it. This prepares you for Study Session 3, where the trust that makes an executive rely on your judgment at all becomes the direct focus.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Look at a recent document you wrote. Did its main point appear first, or did a reader have to reach the end to find it? 2. Rewrite the opening of one document you know well as a single governing sentence, with supporting points grouped beneath it. Practical Output: Practical Output One briefing document restructured as a pyramid, with the governing recommendation stated first and supporting points grouped into clear categories beneath it. 7.0 References and Further Reading Minto, B. (1987). The Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing and Thinking. London: Minto International. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Ecclesiastes 12:10, on the Preacher seeking words of delight, written in uprightness and words of truth. Qur'an, Surah An-Nisa 4:63, on speaking a far-reaching, effective word.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: The Trust That Makes the Role Possible

blocks.text: Introduction Chantal Ngaifei, widowed four years earlier and now the sole person her executive trusted with the organization's most sensitive personnel matters, once let slip, in a moment of casual friendliness with a colleague, a detail she had assumed was harmless. It was not. This session explores what trust in a discretionary role actually rests on, and how a single lapse can shake it even when everything else about the relationship remains genuinely strong. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain the components of trust relevant to a discretionary role. Distinguish ability, benevolence and integrity as separate bases of trust. Handle sensitive information without over-sharing or under-communicating. Recognise when withholding information itself damages trust. Rebuild trust after a real lapse. Maintain consistent discretion under social pressure to share. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Detail That Was Not Actually Harmless Chantal Ngaifei supports the country director of a humanitarian organization in Bangui, and for two years her discretion with sensitive staffing and donor information had been, by every account, excellent. In one relaxed conversation with a colleague she liked and trusted, she mentioned a personnel detail she assumed was already widely known. It was not. Her director learned of the disclosure from someone else, and the ease between them changed noticeably for weeks afterward. 2.2 What Trust Is Actually Built From In 1995, the researchers Roger Mayer, James Davis and F. David Schoorman published a study in the Academy of Management Review proposing an integrative model of organizational trust, built on three distinct components. Ability is a person's competence to do what is expected. Benevolence is a genuine concern for the other party's wellbeing beyond self-interest. Integrity is adherence to principles the other party finds acceptable, including consistency and honesty. Their central finding was that trust depends on all three, and a lapse in even one, an unexpected slip in integrity, for instance, can damage trust significantly even where ability and benevolence remain fully intact. 2.3 Protecting Trust Deliberately Distinguishing What Is Actually Sensitive From What Merely Feels Casual Information that feels harmless in a friendly moment is not automatically harmless; checking, before sharing anything, whether a detail is actually meant to stay contained is a habit, not a one-time judgment call. Communicating Enough Without Over-Sharing Withholding all information indiscriminately can itself damage trust, since colleagues need enough clarity to do their own work; the goal is precise discretion, not blanket silence. Rebuilding Trust Deliberately After a Real Lapse A genuine lapse is not repaired by simply being more careful going forward; naming the lapse honestly, understanding exactly what made it damaging, and demonstrating consistent discretion over time is what actually rebuilds it. 2.4 Key Practices Check whether a detail is actually meant to stay contained before sharing it, even in a casual moment. Distinguish over-sharing from appropriate, necessary communication. Notice when withholding information itself is damaging trust, not just protecting it. Name a real lapse honestly rather than simply hoping it is forgotten. Rebuild trust through consistent discretion demonstrated over time, not through a single gesture. 2.5 A Worked Example: Chantal's Repair After the disclosure, Chantal did not wait for the tension to fade on its own. She raised it directly with her director, naming exactly what she had shared and why she had mistakenly believed it was already known, without minimizing what had happened. She did not change her actual approach to discretion, which had genuinely been strong. She became more deliberate about a single habit, pausing before any casual conversation touching organizational matters to ask herself whether a detail was actually hers to share. Six months of consistent discretion, not any single apology, was what genuinely restored the working ease between her and her director. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Assuming that strong discretion in general excuses a single lapse, or that time alone will repair a damaged sense of trust without any direct acknowledgment, is the mistake that prolongs the damage of an otherwise isolated incident. Trust built over years can still be shaken by one moment of carelessness, and pretending otherwise usually slows the actual repair. 2.7 Named, Then Rebuilt Chantal's working relationship with her director recovered on the timeline of the honesty she brought to it, not on the timeline of simply waiting for the awkwardness to fade, which is a distinction this session asks you to hold onto the next time a lapse of your own needs addressing rather than outwaiting. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned that trust in a discretionary role rests on ability, benevolence and integrity together, and how to rebuild it deliberately after a real lapse. This prepares you for Study Session 4, where that same trust underpins your work as the gatekeeper between an executive and the outside world.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a piece of information you handle regularly. Is it actually meant to stay contained, or have you assumed that without checking? 2. Name one habit you could build to pause before sharing organizational details in casual conversation. Practical Output: Practical Output A short written reflection naming one category of sensitive information she handles, and one specific habit to protect it more deliberately. 7.0 References and Further Reading Mayer, R.C., Davis, J.H., & Schoorman, F.D. (1995). An integrative model of organizational trust. Academy of Management Review, 20(3), 709 to 734. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 11:13, on the trustworthy in spirit keeping a confidence covered. Qur'an, Surah At-Tahrim 66:3, on a confided matter and what follows when it is disclosed.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: Halima's director asked her why a routine vendor invoice needed his personal sign-off. What was the underlying issue?
options: The invoice contained an error
Halima was forwarding routine items that did not actually need his judgment
The vendor was new and unapproved
The budget line had not yet been approved
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Deciding What Actually Needs Her) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Drucker's 1966 argument, what should an effective executive's attention be protected for?
options: Every decision, regardless of its nature
The small number of decisions and relationships that genuinely require their own judgment
Only routine, low-stakes matters
Nothing; executives should delegate all decisions
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Deciding What Actually Needs Her) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session identify as the real problem with forwarding every item to an executive?
options: It shows genuine thoroughness
It fails to provide the triage the role exists to offer, treating every item as equally deserving of attention
It always speeds up decision-making
It has no real effect on an executive's schedule
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Deciding What Actually Needs Her) before continuing.

quiz.q: Yves's executive often stopped reading his briefings partway through. What was the underlying cause?
options: The briefings contained factual errors
The actual recommendation appeared only in the closing paragraph, after background the executive did not have time to finish
The executive disliked reading briefings in general
The briefings were too short
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Leading With the Conclusion) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Minto's 1987 Pyramid Principle, how does the mind naturally organize information?
options: As an unstructured list with no groupings
Into pyramidal groupings under a single governing point
Purely chronologically, in the order information is received
Randomly, with no natural structure at all
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Leading With the Conclusion) before continuing.

quiz.q: What does this session recommend stating in the very first sentence of a briefing?
options: The full background history
The governing conclusion or recommendation
A list of every person consulted
A question for the reader to answer
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Leading With the Conclusion) before continuing.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Standing at the Door

blocks.text: Introduction Hicham Bennani thought his job was simply to say yes or no to people requesting his executive's time, until he realized that every one of those decisions was also quietly shaping how outsiders understood his executive's priorities. This session teaches you to do both jobs at once, filtering what comes in and representing what your executive actually stands for. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain the two core functions of a boundary-spanning role. Filter incoming requests without alienating important relationships. Represent an executive's priorities accurately to outsiders. Recognise when a gatekeeping decision should be escalated rather than made independently. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 More Than a Yes or No Hicham Bennani manages access to a government ministry director in Rabat, and for his first year he treated every incoming request the same simple way, approve it or decline it based on the calendar. A frustrated stakeholder, denied a meeting for the third time with no real explanation, complained publicly that the ministry seemed uninterested in his sector entirely, a perception Hicham's brisk, unexplained declines had unintentionally created. 2.2 A Role That Faces Two Directions at Once In 1977, the researchers Howard Aldrich and Diane Herker published Boundary Spanning Roles and Organization Structure in the Academy of Management Review, describing roles that sit at an organization's boundary as performing two distinct functions simultaneously. The first is information processing, filtering and translating what comes in from outside. The second is external representation, shaping how the organization itself is perceived by whoever sits on the other side of that boundary. Their point is that a boundary role is never neutral; every filtering decision also represents the organization, whether or not that is intended. 2.3 Managing Both Functions Deliberately Filtering Without Alienating Declining a request without explanation leaves the requester to fill in the reason themselves, often with an assumption worse than the truth; a brief, honest reason preserves the relationship even when the answer is no. Representing Priorities Accurately, Not Just Politely What an assistant says, and how, about an executive's availability and interests genuinely shapes an outsider's understanding of what that executive actually cares about, which makes accuracy as important as courtesy. Recognising the Genuinely Escalation-Worthy Case A request that touches a sensitive relationship, an unusual circumstance, or real ambiguity about priority belongs with the executive directly, rather than being resolved unilaterally at the door. 2.4 Key Practices Give a brief, honest reason when declining a request, rather than a bare refusal. Recognise that every filtering decision also represents the executive to whoever is on the other side. Escalate requests that touch sensitive relationships or genuine ambiguity, rather than deciding alone. Check periodically whether your filtering patterns match what the executive actually intends. 2.5 A Worked Example: Hicham's Revised Approach After the public complaint, Hicham changed how he declined requests, adding a brief, honest reason to every refusal, this quarter's calendar is fully committed to the budget review, but I would be glad to schedule November, rather than a bare no. For genuinely ambiguous cases, a stakeholder request that seemed to touch a sensitive ongoing negotiation, he began checking directly with his director rather than deciding alone. Within two months, the same stakeholder who had complained publicly told a colleague that the ministry's office, while still selective about time, at least explained itself honestly, a small shift that mattered more than Hicham had expected. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Treating gatekeeping as a simple yes or no decision, without recognising that every declined request also shapes how outsiders understand the organization, is the mistake that quietly damages relationships a purely transactional approach never accounts for. A closed door explained is very different, to the person standing outside it, from a closed door left unexplained. 2.7 What the Door Actually Represents Nothing about Hicham's approval rate changed once he began explaining his declines. What changed was how accurately his door represented a director stakeholders had, until then, mostly had to guess about. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned that a gatekeeping role filters information and represents the executive simultaneously, and that both functions deserve deliberate attention. This prepares you for Study Session 5, where the same realistic judgment shapes how you plan executive travel and complex logistics.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a recent request you declined on someone's behalf. Did you explain the reason, or leave it unexplained? 2. Name one category of request you currently decide alone that might actually deserve escalation. Practical Output: Practical Output A short set of guidelines naming how she will explain declined requests and which categories of request she will escalate rather than decide alone. 7.0 References and Further Reading Aldrich, H.E., & Herker, D. (1977). Boundary spanning roles and organization structure. Academy of Management Review, 2(2), 217 to 230. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: John 10:3, on the gatekeeper opening the door and the sheep hearing his voice. Qur'an, Surah An-Nur 24:27, on not entering a home before ascertaining welcome and greeting its inhabitants.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Planning for the Trip That Won't Go as Planned

blocks.text: Introduction Marie-Ange Confiance, who is hard of hearing and relies on captioned calls and written confirmations for much of her logistics coordination, had planned executive travel connections down to the minute for years, certain her plans were realistic, until a pattern of near-missed connections made her go back and actually check her assumptions against what had really happened each time. Planning travel and complex logistics the way things actually go, rather than the way a plan on paper suggests they will, is the skill this session builds. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain why planners reliably underestimate how long complex logistics take. Build realistic buffers into a travel or logistics plan. Distinguish a best-case plan from a realistic one. Use past experience, not just the current plan, to estimate timing. Adjust a plan when early signs suggest it is falling behind. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Plan That Looked Perfect on Paper Marie-Ange Confiance coordinates travel for a tourism board executive based in Victoria, and for years she built connection times using the shortest realistic estimate for each leg, an hour for customs, forty minutes for a transfer, confident these numbers reflected genuine experience. A string of near-missed connections over several months, each blamed at the time on unusual circumstances, prompted her to finally compare her planned times against what had actually happened on every trip that year. 2.2 Why Plans Underestimate Reality In 1994, the researchers Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin and Michael Ross published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology examining what they called the planning fallacy, the tendency for people to underestimate how long their own tasks will actually take. Their research found that people focus on an idealized version of a plan rather than on relevant past experience when making predictions, and that this bias persists even when a person has direct, personal history of similar tasks taking longer than planned. Their study documented students underestimating a project's completion time by nearly two-thirds, despite knowing from experience that similar projects usually ran late. 2.3 Planning From Experience, Not Just the Best Case Checking Past Experience Before Trusting a New Estimate Reviewing how long a similar connection, transfer or process has actually taken in the past, rather than relying on an idealized best-case number, produces a far more realistic plan. Building In Realistic Buffers, Not Minimal Ones Adding time specifically for the kind of delay that has happened before, not just a token few minutes, protects a plan against the same fallacy that shrinks every estimate toward the best case. Watching for Early Signs a Plan Is Falling Behind Noticing early indicators, a delayed departure, a longer than usual queue, and adjusting the remaining plan immediately, prevents a small early delay from becoming a missed connection later. 2.4 Key Practices Check how long a similar task actually took in the past before trusting a new estimate. Build realistic buffers based on real history, not a token few minutes. Distinguish a best-case plan from a realistic one, and plan around the realistic one. Watch for early signs that a plan is falling behind, and adjust immediately. Record actual outcomes after each trip to improve future planning. 2.5 A Worked Example: Marie-Ange's Buffer Rebuild When Marie-Ange finally compared her planned times against her own trip records, she found her actual average customs clearance time was closer to ninety minutes than the sixty she had been planning around, and her transfer buffer had been adequate only when nothing at all went wrong. She rebuilt her standard planning template using these real averages, not her original best-case estimates, and added a specific, named buffer for the kind of disruption that had actually occurred before. The near-missed connections stopped, not because travel itself became more predictable, but because her plan finally reflected what travel had actually, repeatedly, been like. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Trusting an idealized best-case estimate over a person's own documented history of delays is the bias that quietly undermines even careful, experienced planners at this stage, because the best-case number always feels more reasonable in the moment than the messier reality. A plan built on how things are supposed to go, rather than how they have actually gone, is a plan built to fail under ordinary pressure. 2.7 Matching the Record, Not the Hope Nothing about air travel became more predictable for Marie-Ange. Her plans simply stopped pretending it already was, and started matching what her own records had been quietly showing her all along. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to plan travel and complex logistics around realistic estimates grounded in past experience, rather than an idealized best case. This closes the operational core of the course and prepares you for Study Session 6, where anticipating needs before being asked brings every earlier session together.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think of a recent plan you made that ran later than expected. What did you estimate it would take, and what did it actually take? 2. Name one recurring task in your own planning where you could check real past experience before trusting your next estimate. Practical Output: Practical Output One travel or logistics plan rebuilt with time estimates checked against real past experience, including at least one named, realistic buffer. 7.0 References and Further Reading Buehler, R., Griffin, D., & Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the planning fallacy: Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366 to 381. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Luke 14:31-32, on a king considering carefully whether his forces can withstand an opposing army before committing to war. Qur'an, Surah Al-Hashr 59:18, on every soul looking to what it has put forth for tomorrow.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Knowing Before Being Asked

blocks.text: Introduction Nomsa Simelane, raising her daughter alone while supporting a regional director in Mbabane, had always prided herself on responding quickly and well to whatever her director asked for. It was only when a colleague pointed out how often she anticipated needs before they were even voiced that Nomsa realized responding well and anticipating well were not, in fact, the same skill. This final session brings every earlier session in this course together into the capability that makes an assistant genuinely indispensable, knowing what is needed before being asked. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what distinguishes proactive behavior from simply responding well. Anticipate a need based on patterns rather than waiting for an explicit request. Take reasonable initiative without overstepping. Sustain anticipatory support without becoming presumptuous. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Fast, But Always Reactive Nomsa Simelane supports a regional director for a financial services firm in Mbabane, and for two years she prided herself on responding quickly to every request, often within minutes of it being made. A new colleague, watching her work for a week, remarked that Nomsa seemed to have documents ready before her director even asked for them, a pattern Nomsa herself had never actually named or noticed she was doing. 2.2 A Distinct, Learnable Capability In 2008, the researchers Adam Grant and Susan Ashford published The Dynamics of Proactivity at Work in Research in Organizational Behavior, arguing that proactive behavior, anticipating and acting ahead of a future need rather than simply responding well once it arises, is a distinct capability with its own specific psychological drivers, not merely a byproduct of being generally responsive or competent. Their framework distinguishes proactive behavior by three features: it is anticipatory, future focused rather than reactive; change oriented, aimed at improving a situation rather than maintaining it; and self-initiated, undertaken without being explicitly instructed. 2.3 Anticipating Deliberately, Not Just Responding Fast Noticing the Patterns That Predict a Future Need Recognising that a director always requests the same supporting document before a certain kind of meeting, and preparing it before being asked, turns a repeated request into an anticipated one. Taking Initiative Within a Reasonable, Trusted Scope Anticipatory action works within boundaries a director has come to trust, not by making decisions or commitments the director has not actually authorized. Checking, Not Assuming, When a Pattern Genuinely Shifts Confirming with a brief question when circumstances suggest a usual pattern may not apply this time prevents anticipation from tipping into presumption. 2.4 Key Practices Notice recurring patterns that predict a future need, not just requests as they arrive. Prepare for an anticipated need within a scope the executive has come to trust. Confirm with a brief question when a usual pattern seems likely to shift. Distinguish genuine anticipation from simply responding quickly once asked. 2.5 A Worked Example: Nomsa's Named Pattern Once her colleague named what she was doing, Nomsa examined her own habits more deliberately. She noticed she always prepared a specific budget summary before her director's monthly finance committee meeting, a document he had stopped needing to request explicitly months earlier, because it was simply always ready. She began applying the same deliberate noticing elsewhere, recognising that a particular kind of travel request typically followed a particular kind of client meeting, and preparing the groundwork a day in advance. When a pattern genuinely seemed likely to shift, a client relationship ending, for instance, she checked directly rather than assuming the usual preparation still applied. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Treating fast, competent responses to explicit requests as the ceiling of the role, without ever noticing or naming the recurring patterns that could be anticipated instead, is the habit that keeps a capable assistant reactive indefinitely. Responding well to what is asked and anticipating what will be needed are related, but they are not the same skill, and only one of them is learned by simply working faster. 2.7 Known Before Asked Nomsa's work is not busier for the anticipation built into it now. It simply arrives, more often than not, already understood, which is the same quiet thread running back through every session this course has offered, deciding what needs attention, shaping what gets prepared, protecting the trust that makes any of it possible, and finally, noticing before being told. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to distinguish proactive anticipation from fast reaction, and to build the habit of noticing patterns that predict a future need. This closes Course 96 and prepares you for Course 97, Meeting and Board Support for Executives.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Name one recurring request you currently wait for, that you could learn to anticipate instead. 2. Think of one pattern in your own work where a need has shifted recently. How would you check rather than assume? Practical Output: Practical Output A short written account naming one genuinely anticipated need she now prepares for in advance, and one pattern she checks rather than assumes. 7.0 References and Further Reading Grant, A.M., & Ashford, S.J. (2008). The dynamics of proactivity at work. Research in Organizational Behavior, 28, 3 to 34. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 22:3, on the prudent seeing danger and hiding himself, while the simple go on and suffer for it. Qur'an, Surah Al-Anfal 8:60, on preparing whatever one is able of strength and readiness in advance.

quiz.q: A stakeholder complained publicly after being declined a meeting for the third time with no explanation. What did this reveal about Hicham's approach?
options: His declines were factually incorrect
His unexplained refusals had unintentionally shaped a negative perception of the ministry
The stakeholder's complaint was entirely unrelated to Hicham's decisions
The ministry director had personally caused the complaint
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Standing at the Door) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Aldrich and Herker's 1977 research, what two functions do boundary-spanning roles perform simultaneously?
options: Scheduling and budgeting
Information processing and external representation
Hiring and training
Marketing and sales
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Standing at the Door) before continuing.

quiz.q: Why does this session argue that a boundary role is never neutral?
options: Because boundary roles have no real function
Because every filtering decision also represents the organization, whether or not that is intended
Because boundary roles only process information, never represent anyone
Because neutrality is always the correct approach
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Standing at the Door) before continuing.

quiz.q: Marie-Ange's connection times looked realistic on paper but led to a string of near-missed connections. What did comparing her plans against her actual trip records reveal?
options: Her plans had always been perfectly accurate
Her actual customs clearance time was closer to ninety minutes than the sixty she had planned around
The airports themselves were entirely unpredictable and unplannable
Her transfer buffers had always been too generous
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Planning for the Trip That Won't Go as Planned) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Buehler, Griffin and Ross's 1994 research on the planning fallacy, what do people typically focus on when predicting how long a task will take?
options: Relevant past experience with similar tasks
An idealized version of the plan rather than past experience
Advice from other people exclusively
Random guessing with no real basis
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Planning for the Trip That Won't Go as Planned) before continuing.

quiz.q: What did the 1994 study find about students' predictions, even when they had experience with similar past delays?
options: Their predictions were always accurate
They still underestimated completion time significantly, despite their own history of delays
They always overestimated how long a task would take
Past experience made no difference because they had none
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Planning for the Trip That Won't Go as Planned) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Halima's director asked her why a routine vendor invoice needed his personal sign-off. What was the underlying issue?

Halima was forwarding routine items that did not actually need his judgment
The vendor was new and unapproved
The budget line had not yet been approved

finalQuiz.q: According to Drucker's 1966 argument, what should an effective executive's attention be protected for?
options: Every decision, regardless of its nature
The small number of decisions and relationships that genuinely require their own judgment
Only routine, low-stakes matters
Nothing; executives should delegate all decisions
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Deciding What Actually Needs Her) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session identify as the real problem with forwarding every item to an executive?
options: It shows genuine thoroughness
It fails to provide the triage the role exists to offer, treating every item as equally deserving of attention
It always speeds up decision-making
It has no real effect on an executive's schedule
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Deciding What Actually Needs Her) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: Yves's executive often stopped reading his briefings partway through. What was the underlying cause?
options: The briefings contained factual errors
The actual recommendation appeared only in the closing paragraph, after background the executive did not have time to finish
The executive disliked reading briefings in general
The briefings were too short

finalQuiz.q: According to Minto's 1987 Pyramid Principle, how does the mind naturally organize information?

Into pyramidal groupings under a single governing point
Purely chronologically, in the order information is received
Randomly, with no natural structure at all

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend stating in the very first sentence of a briefing?
options: The full background history
The governing conclusion or recommendation
A list of every person consulted
A question for the reader to answer

She was immediately dismissed from her position
The colleague reported her to an external authority

Trust can be significantly damaged, even where the other components remain fully intact
Only ability actually matters for trust
Integrity has no real connection to trust
